title: ashes, and forty days
hookLine: a smudge on the forehead, fish on Friday: giving something up is a way of paying attention

cards: One Wednesday a year, a coworker shows up with a black smudge on her forehead. Then the barista. Then a kid on the train.

Somebody leans over to say: you've got something on your face. It's Ash Wednesday, and it starts a season. For the next forty days, a Catholic friend might be off chocolate, or off social media, or eating fish on Fridays.
It can look like a diet. It isn't about the chocolate.

teach.b: Lent is the season of forty days before Easter.
Forty is the number the Bible keeps reaching for when someone is being tested: Noah's rain, Moses on the mountain, and Jesus fasting in the desert for forty days before he begins his work.
Lent walks alongside those forty days. It opens with ash.
A cross is traced on the forehead, often with words from the Bible's first pages, in the Douay-Rheims: "dust thou art, and into dust thou shalt return." It sounds grim.
Catholics hear it as honest: you won't be here forever, so what will you do with the time?
Then come three old practices: prayer, fasting, and giving to the poor. Catholics fast on Ash Wednesday and Good Friday, and skip meat on the Fridays of Lent, because Friday is the day Jesus died.
The rule doesn't count fish as meat. Hello, Friday fish fry. Many also give something up.

Here's the idea underneath: give up something small, and every reach for it becomes a moment of noticing. The empty space where the chocolate was becomes a little room for prayer, or for someone else.
And the forty days only make sense because of where they end: Easter morning.

how: Catholics receive ashes on Ash Wednesday, fast on Ash Wednesday and Good Friday, abstain from meat on Fridays in Lent, and take on prayer, fasting and almsgiving for the forty days before Easter.

games.q: it's Lent, and you gave up coffee. it's 3 p.m. and you reach for a cup out of habit. in the idea this lesson describes, what's that moment for?
o: to prove you're stronger than other people.
to notice, and let the reach become a reminder.
games.why: the reach becomes a reminder: of God, of someone else, of what you actually want your time for.

games.q: put back the three old practices of Lent.

practice: Three breaths with the bell. Think of one small thing you reach for without thinking: your phone, a snack, a complaint. Picture yourself reaching for it and stopping, hand in the air.
Stay in that pause for three slow breaths, and see what you notice there instead.

wordCard.voice: Lent. Forty days before Easter, of prayer, fasting and giving, where less becomes a way of paying attention. Sixth word.

orig.note: Latin: the fortieth. the Church's Latin name for Lent, still behind Spanish cuaresma and Italian quaresima.

carryVoice: Your line: less, on purpose. The ash says the time is short; the empty space makes room. Day six, done.
